questions.question: How is the paper's Gaussian noise model described at the pixel level?

options.A: Each noisy pixel is the true value plus a random Gaussian-distributed value
options.B: Each pixel is replaced by one of two extrema with equal probability
options.C: Noise multiplies the pixel and follows a gamma distribution
options.D: Noise is generated by integrating a spatially white process over distance

questions.rationale: The paper describes additive Gaussian perturbations and gives mean and standard deviation as distribution parameters.
questions.evidence_quote: each pixel in the noisy image is the sum of the true pixel value and a random Gaussian distributed noise value.

questions.question: Which property distinguishes the paper's salt-and-pepper noise description from its Gaussian model?

options.A: Corrupted pixels take only minimum or maximum intensity values while unaffected pixels remain unchanged
options.B: Every pixel receives an additive bell-distributed perturbation
options.C: The corruption is multiplicative and gamma distributed throughout the image
options.D: Pixel errors are spatially correlated as integrated white noise

questions.rationale: The impulse noise has two extrema (0 and 255 in 8-bit images) and leaves other pixels untouched.

questions.question: In what imaging settings does the article associate speckle noise with a multiplicative process?

options.A: Coherent systems such as laser, acoustic, and SAR imagery, due to interference among coherent returns
options.B: Only digital photography, due to out-of-focus optics
options.C: Binary computer-vision images, due to quantization into one bit
options.D: Remote-sensing images only when atmospheric turbulence is absent

questions.rationale: The review attributes speckle to random interference between coherent returns and lists coherent imaging modalities.
questions.evidence_quote: This type of noise occurs in almost all coherent imaging systems such as laser, acoustics and SAR

questions.question: How does the article characterize Brownian noise relative to white noise?

options.A: It is a special case of 1/f noise obtained by integrating white noise
options.B: It is white noise passed through a high-pass filter
options.C: It is a two-level impulse process whose variance is independent of frequency
options.D: It is an additive Gaussian process with stationary independent pixels

questions.rationale: The review identifies Brownian noise as fractal/nonstationary 1/f noise and describes its construction by integration.
questions.evidence_quote: Brownian noise is a special case of 1/f noise. It is obtained by integrating white noise.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off the review attributes to conventional spatial filters?

options.A: They can suppress noise but often blur images and erase edges
options.B: They preserve all edges but amplify high-frequency noise
options.C: They require exact wavelet coefficients but reduce computational overhead
options.D: They remove only multiplicative noise and cannot handle Gaussian noise

questions.rationale: The authors say low-pass spatial methods remove noise reasonably but at the cost of blurring edges and detail.
questions.evidence_quote: Generally spatial filters remove noise to a reasonable extent but at the cost of blurring images

questions.question: Why does the article say Wiener filtering can perform poorly despite being optimal for Gaussian noise in an MSE sense?

options.A: It needs noise and signal spectra and is most effective for smooth signals; spatial smoothing can blur sharp details
options.B: It requires a binary image and cannot operate on grayscale pixels
options.C: It assumes multiplicative gamma noise and therefore fails on Gaussian noise
options.D: Its threshold is independent of image size and always too small

questions.rationale: The review notes both its spectral-information requirement and its tendency to smooth edges and fine detail.
questions.evidence_quote: The wiener filtering [11] method requires the information about the spectra of the noise and the original signal

questions.question: What artifact does the review associate specifically with hard wavelet coefficient thresholding?

options.A: Spurious blips caused when moderately large noise coefficients are not removed
options.B: A uniform loss of all coefficients above the threshold
options.C: Pseudo-Gibbs oscillations uniquely caused by translation invariance
options.D: Artificial frequency peaks caused by choosing a Fourier cutoff

questions.rationale: Hard thresholding leaves coefficients above the cutoff untouched, and the text identifies resulting spurious blips as artifacts.
questions.evidence_quote: the method generates spurious blips, better known as artifacts

questions.question: Why can VISU Shrink oversmooth images according to the comparison?

options.A: Its universal threshold depends on the number of data points and can become unwarrantedly large
options.B: It uses a generalized Gaussian prior that always suppresses low-frequency coefficients
options.C: It replaces every coefficient with a neighborhood average
options.D: It is shift invariant and therefore removes all image edges

questions.rationale: The non-adaptive threshold scales with image sample count, which can make it too large and over-smooth the image.
questions.evidence_quote: its threshold choice can be unwarrantedly large due to its dependence on the number of pixels in the image.

questions.question: What limitation of coefficient-magnitude-only classification is highlighted at high noise levels?

options.A: Noise may exceed signal magnitudes, so neighboring coefficient spatial configuration becomes informative
options.B: Signal coefficients become exactly Gaussian, making MSE undefined
options.C: The wavelet transform ceases to map white noise to white noise
options.D: The coefficient tree loses all parent-child relations at high noise

questions.rationale: The article notes that magnitude alone fails when noise is stronger than signal; coherent spatial structures can help distinguish signal from random scatter.
questions.evidence_quote: The assumption that one can distinguish noise from the signal solely based on coefficient magnitudes is violated when noise levels are higher than signal magnitudes.

questions.question: At 90% noise density on the grayscale Lena image, which listed filter achieved the highest PSNR and IEF in Table I?
questions.rationale: MDBUTMF is the largest entry in both reported metrics at the stated 90% noise density.
